extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in social criticism, culture, and Victorian essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of the essay's evaluative criteria about 'civilization' and humanization — the powers, indicators, and social effects the author uses to judge nations and classes. Useful for understanding standards of a civilized society as argued in a Victorian cultural-critique essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The power of conduct is the greatest of all.' — moral conduct (sense for conduct) is the central element of humanization and civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author treats conduct as primary: nations must cultivate moral behaviour and public spirit. Examples/contrast: France is praised for social life but criticized for lacking sufficient moral reform (Michelet on the Reformation failing in France). Anti-patterns: strong social manners without conduct leads to demoralization and 'intellectual stoppage.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The power of intellect and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The power of knowledge, in the same way, is eminently an influence with the Germans.' — a nation needs a sense for knowing 'scientifically' and systematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion emphasizes scientific, systematic knowledge and rational method. The author contrasts German strength here with other nations' weaknesses. Guidance includes that knowing 'scientifically' is different from mere general culture; it requires regular right processes of knowledge. Lack of this power weakens civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The taste for beauty and art is a distinct power in humanization; Italians historically revived and pursued beauty and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public taste and popular ability to judge beauty (examples: Italians saying 'e bello'/'e brutto') are indicators. Cultivation of art and a public appreciation for beauty lift civilization. Anti-patterns: materialized classes that 'dabble' in art without genuine pursuit of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power of social life and manners (l'esprit de société)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social intercourse and humane manners form a major power of civilization; they promote equality by making men feel equal in daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Voltaire's identification of Louis XIV's age gift as 'l'esprit de société' and praises French social manners for enabling conversation across classes. Guidance: humane manners bring people together, foster consideration and mutual understanding. Anti-patterns: absence of such manners produces social partition between classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality as a promoter of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality spreads humane life and social civilization widely — France's equality brought widespread refinement and agreeable life to many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality is presented as a mechanism that diffuses the benefits of manners, tastes, and humane life throughout classes. Caveat: equality alone is not sufficient for full humanization; it may coexist with other failings that produce 'fearful troubles.' Historical example: equality helped produce the French Revolution and civilized social life but did not guarantee moral or intellectual depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full humanization requires multiple powers together
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilization (true humanization) demands not one but several powers together: conduct, intellect/knowledge, beauty, and social life/manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding firmly to only one element (e.g., social manners) while neglecting others yields incomplete civilization; the author uses France as an example: strong social life but inadequate conduct, intellect, and beauty produced dangers. Assessment of civilization must therefore weigh all powers, not a single trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of national civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical signs to judge a nation's civilization include public spirit, love of public order and stability, distribution of material well-being, popular taste for beauty, strength of intellect/knowledge, and manners across classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author assesses England, France, Germany, Italy by these indicators: England — energy, honesty, strong sense for conduct, splendid aristocracy but class-based uncivilizedness; France — wide diffusion of manners and refinement among peasants; Germany — scientific seriousness. Use multiple social facts (e.g., peasant manners, theatrical standards, public appreciation of art) to form judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material effects of inequality on civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The social constitution of inequality 'materializes' the upper class, 'vulgarizes' the middle class, and 'brutalizes' the lower class, thereby obstructing civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a causal evaluative criterion: measure how class inequality shapes tastes, manners, and ideals. Examples: English aristocracy becomes materialized and disconnected from real social function; middle class falls into Puritan narrowness or vulgar imitation; lower class resorts to 'beer, gin, and fun.' Anti-patterns: high inequality accompanied by admiration of material splendor rather than humane ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and deficiencies of classes as civilization criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the civilizing capacity of social classes: aristocracy (can set manners but may be materialized), class of gentlemen (cultivated and important civilizing force), middle class (divided into serious and rowdy portions), and lower class (measure their manners and tastes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class behaviour to predict cultural outcomes: a cultivated 'class of gentlemen' promotes intellect and beauty; a materialized aristocracy may fail in spiritual leadership; middle-class Puritanism can create ennui and narrowness; compare regions (e.g., Scotland vs England) to gauge class effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of overemphasizing one power (Puritanism critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overemphasis on conduct alone (Puritan temper/narrow Biblism) leads to 'hideousness' and 'immense ennui' by neglecting beauty, intellect, and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author illustrates with historical acts (Puritan Parliament burning pictures) and literary examples (Milton's harsh disputations). As an evaluative rule: suspicion toward cultures that prize conduct while suppressing art, open intellect, and humane manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of well-being must be higher than mere material comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Socialistic/communistic schemes that set too low and material a standard of well-being fail because human instinct for perfection rebels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging social programs or ideals, assess whether they elevate human aspirations beyond mere material sufficiency. Examples: M. de Laveleye's account of France shows material well-being widespread, but the ideal must not be 'lowered and coarsened' for broader sharing to count as true humanization.
